correctness.rationale: The proof works over the axioms, independently of any coordinatization. Two monochromatic lines have the same colour at the intersection. For each point outside their union, joining it to a point on the first line away from the intersection produces a line containing two points of the common colour, forcing the outside point to have that colour. With no monochromatic line, the unique line through any pair separates the colours. With one such line, any repetition off it forces a second monochromatic line, either by joining two off-line points with the same colour, or by joining an off-line point of the line colour to a point on the line. Conversely each other line meets the designated line once and is rainbow. Choosing the distinguished line and assigning colours injectively to the classes gives n(t)_(q²+1), which is the second displayed term including the empty palette; the injective type gives (t)_n. Thus the named and unnamed optimal counts and q−1 gaps follow. The incidence-degree counterexample is correct under the standard incidence meaning of vertex degree: q+1 versus q²+q in the complete two-section. The source corollary says greatest vertex degree, not literally incidence degree; its proof conflates the two, and the result does not refute the corrected two-section interpretation. The packaged finite checker was inspected, not replayed; the unrestricted incidence proof and counts were reconstructed directly.
